item.title: OpenCode Quickstart: Install, Configure, and Run the Terminal Agent
item.description: OpenCode is an open-source terminal-first agentic coder: TUI on bare invocation, one-shot opencode run for scripts, headless opencode serve with web UI, programmatic control through the official JS/TS SDK — all provider-flexible from cloud APIs to local Ollama. Install, verify, connect, run real workflows: the whole ramp in one page.

item.title: Oh My Opencode Quickstart: Install, Configure, Run Ultrawork
item.description: Oh My Opencode turns OpenCode into a multi-agent harness: Sisyphus orchestrating specialists in parallel behind the ultrawork keyword. Install the plugin, verify three things, learn the two concepts that matter — mode switch plus specialist routing — and tune concurrency before billing surprises arrive.

item.title: Oh My Opencode Agents: Sisyphus and the Specialist Crew
item.description: The biggest capability jump in OpenCode comes from separating orchestration, planning, execution, and research into specialist agents. Oh My Opencode packages that into a batteries-included harness: Sisyphus coordinating eleven agents with distinct permissions, prompts, and model preferences — where changing an agent’s model changes which prompt fires.

item.title: Oh My Opencode in Practice: When Orchestration Pays and When It Bills
item.description: Oh My Opencode promises a virtual AI dev team — Sisyphus orchestrating specialists in parallel behind one ultrawork keyword. The promise holds for the right workload and taxes everything else: tripled tokens on single-window tasks, five-figure startup context, and at least one incident where a looping subagent billed hundreds unsupervised. Hands-on results plus community data below.

item.title: Text Embeddings for RAG and Search: Ollama and OpenAI-Compatible APIs
item.description: An embedding is a fixed-dimensional float vector placing similar meanings nearby — a representation layer for search, clustering, dedup, and RAG retrieval, not token IDs and not chat output. The concepts stay identical across backends; only the HTTP surface changes. Two local patterns cover nearly everything: Ollama’s embed endpoint and any OpenAI-compatible embeddings route.

item.title: Inspecting and Debugging MCP Servers from the CLI: JSON-RPC, jq, and Shell Helpers
item.description: The fastest way to learn what an MCP server actually does is to talk to it directly, without a model in the loop. The Model Context Protocol speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over a boring transport, so every message you send is printable, greppable, and scriptable. You can list a server’s tools, call one with fixed arguments, diff its contract between versions, and script the checks in CI. This guide covers the stdio transport in depth: the initialize handshake, listing and calling tools, extracting schemas with jq, shell helper functions, a debugging playbook, and what changes when a server speaks Streamable HTTP over curl. All examples were run against the reference filesystem server on macOS.

item.title: Claude Skills for Developers: SKILL.md That Survives Real Work
item.description: Teams misuse Claude Skills two ways: dumping grounds, or giant copy-pasted prompts that never graduate. Both are sloppy. Skills work through progressive disclosure — compact metadata first, full instructions only on task match — letting dozens stay available without bloating every session. Treat them like operations code, not prompt poetry.

item.title: Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM): Design With Deep Context, Review With Fresh Eyes
item.description: Most long AI coding sessions fail the same way: an hour in, the model has absorbed every requirement, every tangent, and every unexamined assumption you both made — and when you finally ask it to review its own work, it reads straight past the gaps it already filled in mentally. Google’s Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) attacks exactly that failure. It splits the job into two roles with opposite memory profiles: a context-rich “Elephant” that drafts the design, and stateless “Goldfish” reviewers that read the draft cold and flag what a fresh reader would trip over.

item.title: Hermes Agent Memory: Two Small Files Beat a Vector Database
item.description: Models are stateless by design: every request independent, no continuity past the context window. Most frameworks bolt memory on afterward — a database to query, a window to stuff. Hermes inverts it: memory isn’t retrieved when needed but injected at every session start, curated, bounded, always active. Two files under 3,600 characters total.

item.title: Agent Memory Providers Compared: Eight Backends for Persistent Agents
item.description: Assistants forget everything at tab-close unless something persists past the context window. Memory providers — services or libraries holding facts and summaries across sessions, usually wired as plugins — keep the framework thin while memory scales. Eight backends cover the space from zero-dependency local to enterprise cloud.

item.title: Building a Self-Evaluating RAG System: Hybrid Search, Routing, and LLM-as-Judge
item.description: Most RAG systems are demos: they retrieve chunks and generate an answer immediately, with no check on whether the retrieved context is relevant, sufficient, or even correct. When retrieval misses, the model hallucinates. There is no recovery loop, no quality signal, and no way to tell which step produced a bad answer. This post documents how to build a self-evaluating RAG system that routes queries, retrieves with hybrid search, and evaluates its own answers using LLM-as-judge. It is built in three cooperating parts: Hybrid search and retrieval — dense + BM25 vectors with int8 quantization in Qdrant, RRF fusion, payload filtering, and multi-year balanced fetch. Agent and MCP — a LangGraph ReAct loop with routing guardrails, wrapped in FastMCP and exposed through a Streamlit UI. Observability and evaluation — Arize Phoenix tracing plus LLM-as-judge scoring for hallucination, QA correctness, and context relevance. The LLM provider layer is shared: Ollama (local llama3.2, nomic-embed-text) or Gemini API (gemini-2.5-flash-lite), switchable via environment variable with no code changes.

item.title: Gatewaying Two DGX Spark vLLM Nodes with vLLM Semantic Router
item.description: You now have two NVIDIA DGX Spark units running vLLM, and you have measured them: one node alone, two nodes behind Nginx load balancing, and two nodes as a Ray cluster. The next question is what sits in front of them: how do you decide which node gets which request, how do you enforce guardrails, and how do you cache repeated queries without hitting the model at all? This post covers vLLM Semantic Router as the gateway layer in front of your two DGX Spark nodes. It selects or combines backends per request based on policy, runs guardrails (jailbreak, PII, hallucination detection), and caches semantically similar queries. We walk through installing it, wiring it to spark-1 and spark-2, defining routes, and adding its metrics to the same Prometheus and Grafana stack you already built.

item.title: Managing Documents with Local LLMs and Self-Hosted Apps
item.description: I stopped relying on cloud AI services for document management. Instead, I run a self-hosted stack of Paperless-ngx, Paperless-GPT, and Paperless AI, backed by local LLMs through Ollama. Nothing leaves my network: academic records, certificates, invoices, tax filings, and receipts all stay on my own hardware. This post documents the stack I built to manage documents locally: how Paperless-ngx serves as the central document hub, how Paperless-GPT handles OCR, how Paperless AI provides RAG-powered chat over the archive, and how everything connects to a local Ollama instance running Qwen 3, MiniCPM-V, and Llama 3.2.

item.title: Monitoring a Self-Hosted LLM Stack: vLLM, Phoenix, and Grafana Measurements
item.description: Running a self-hosted LLM stack produces signals on several axes at once — serving health, per-tenant token consumption, response quality, and full request traces. Classic web monitoring does not capture most of them. Tokens, batching, KV cache pressure, queue dynamics, inter-token latency, and trace spans all need their own measurement. This post is a practical guide to monitoring a self-hosted LLM inference stack. It covers what to measure at each layer (vLLM serving, AI Gateway access, Phoenix tracing and evaluation), which PromQL queries turn raw metrics into dashboards, how KEDA autoscaling consumes the signals, and which SLOs and alerts belong on the platform. The examples assume two NVIDIA DGX Spark units running vLLM, but the metrics and queries apply to any vLLM-based stack.

item.title: Shared KV Cache Across Two DGX Spark Units: Valkey Cluster, Local SSD, and P2P Options
item.description: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark units running independent vLLM instances have a blind spot: vLLM’s prefix cache is per-node. A request landing on spark-2 cannot reuse the KV cache blocks that spark-1 already computed for the same prompt prefix. Every node cold-starts its own KV cache, so repeated prompts and multi-turn conversations pay the prefill penalty on every hop. This post documents how to share KV cache across both DGX Spark nodes using LMCache, a standalone KV cache layer for LLM inference. It compares three native storage backends — a Valkey cluster on both nodes, local SSD per node, and direct P2P transfer over the ConnectX-7 NIC — with no custom Python or dispatcher code required.

item.title: Two DGX Spark 128 GB Units for Local AI: Single Node vs Nginx Load-Balanced vLLM in Grafana
item.description: We bought two NVIDIA DGX Spark units with 128 GB of unified memory each to run large language models locally. Before trusting them with real workloads, we needed to know how they behave under load: one node by itself, two nodes behind a load balancer, and anywhere from one to sixteen people sending requests at the same time. This post is the step-by-step record of how we measured it and how we visualized the results in Grafana. The monitoring stack — Prometheus, Grafana, and the Nginx load balancer — runs on a separate server, while both DGX Spark nodes run independent vLLM instances. It covers preparing the nodes, running vLLM on a single node and across two load-balanced instances, benchmarking with 1, 4, 8, and 16 concurrent users, scraping vLLM metrics into Prometheus, and building the Grafana dashboards that made the comparison readable.

item.title: Two DGX Spark 128 GB Units for Local AI: Single Node vs Ray Clustered vLLM in Grafana
item.description: We bought two NVIDIA DGX Spark units with 128 GB of unified memory each to run large language models locally. Before trusting them with real workloads, we needed to know how they behave under load: one node by itself, two nodes as a Ray cluster with tensor parallelism, and anywhere from one to sixteen people sending requests at the same time. This post is the step-by-step record of how we measured it and how we visualized the results in Grafana. The monitoring stack — Prometheus and Grafana — runs on a separate server, while both DGX Spark nodes run vLLM under a Ray distributed executor. It covers preparing the nodes, running vLLM on a single node and across the Ray cluster, benchmarking with 1, 4, 8, and 16 concurrent users, scraping vLLM metrics into Prometheus, and building the Grafana dashboards that made the comparison readable.

item.title: Kanban in Hermes: Dispatching Agents Without DDoSing Your Own GPU
item.description: Hermes Agent ships a durable Kanban board whose dispatcher happily promotes every ready task at once — fine against elastic cloud APIs, a self-inflicted denial of service against one small GPU cluster. Uncapped promotion floods the gateway with concurrent requests and turns throughput into queueing, thrashing, and timeouts.

item.title: Second Brain for Engineers: Notes Are Storage, Systems Compute
item.description: Overload isn’t volume — it’s unresolved inputs never resurfacing when useful. A second brain externalizes thinking so the biological one spends less on storage and more on interpretation, connection, and output: not a note app, but a loop turning scattered inputs into reusable thinking.

item.title: PKM vs RAG vs Wiki vs Memory: Four Knowledge Jobs, Four Systems
item.description: PKM, wikis, RAG, and AI memory get discussed as rivals solving one problem. They don’t. PKM helps humans think, wikis preserve shared knowledge, RAG retrieves for machines, memory gives agents continuity. Mix them up and you get personal scratch in the wiki, sourceless-truth RAG, database-pretending memory, and automation-bloated PKM.

item.title: LLM Wiki: Compiled Knowledge RAG Cannot Replace
item.description: RAG became the default answer to giving models external knowledge: chunk, embed, retrieve at query time, generate. Useful — and overused. RAG optimizes access, not representation: it finds fragments but builds no stable domain understanding, retrieves context but never decides the canonical explanation. An LLM Wiki moves synthesis to ingest time, compiling sources into structured, linked, human-readable knowledge before any question arrives.

item.title: AI Assistant Architecture: LLM, Memory, Tools, Routing, Observability
item.description: A production assistant isn’t “an LLM with a prompt.” It’s a runtime turning intent into responses and actions through five layers: model, memory, tooling, routing, observability. That split matches provider APIs, MCP, self-hosted runtimes, and real systems alike — and every production disagreement eventually reduces to which context was visible, which tool executed, which model answered, which memory changed, and where the trace says time went.

item.title: Memory Systems in AI Assistants: Working, Structured, Retrieval
item.description: Memory turns assistants from reactive to persistent — and it’s where systems quietly rot. The old short-term/long-term split no longer covers modern agents. The working stack is three layers: working memory for the live run, structured state for durable truth, retrieval memory for supporting evidence — plus a consolidation policy that forgets as deliberately as it remembers.

item.title: Cost Optimization for LLM Systems: Spend Tokens Where They Matter
item.description: Ten thousand requests a day at a cent each is $100 daily — and enterprise scale turns that into five figures fast. Optimization isn’t corner-cutting; it’s spending tokens where they matter. Budgets, fallbacks, local inference break-evens, and caching form the practical stack, roughly in that order of effort.

item.title: vLLM and SGLang: The Community Stories Behind Two Open-Source Inference Engines
item.description: Everyone benchmarks vLLM and SGLang on FLOPS and tokens per second, but the more interesting story is how two academic side projects became the default backends for serving large language models. This post walks through where each engine came from, why they compete, how their contributor bases actually overlap, and what that means for choosing an inference engine in production.

item.title: vLLM Scheduling: How Throughput and Latency Trade Off in Shared Inference
item.description: At 9 in the morning Alice asks the office’s local model to summarize yesterday’s meeting, and the answer streams back faster than she can read it. By 10 the whole team has found the thing. Same GPU, same model — and now everyone’s replies stutter and stall. Something ran out. The hard part is telling what. The short version: the GPU is being shared, and vLLM’s scheduler is good at the sharing part. What usually decides how many people fit is memory space, and long conversations eat most of it. That also tells you which targets to pick for a personal assistant, an office tool, or a customer-facing app.

item.title: Model Routing: Stop Using One Model for Everything
item.description: A 70B model summarizing an email burns money; a 3B model reviewing production code courts disaster. Routing matches task complexity to model capability across four strategies — capability, cost, latency, hybrid — each optimizing what hurts most. Production systems converge on hybrid; start there only after one model genuinely fails.

item.title: LLM Guardrails in Practice: Control the Risk, Not the Model
item.description: Models hallucinate, leak data, emit harmful content, and refuse legitimate requests. Guardrails constrain behavior without removing capability — but only the guardrails that match real risk earn their latency. The discipline is knowing which ones matter and which are noise.

item.title: Multi-Model System Design: The Right Model for the Right Task
item.description: Running a 70B model to summarize an email wastes money; running a 3B model to review production code courts disaster. Multi-model design isn’t about collecting models — it’s about architecture that puts the right model on the right task at the right time, with the simplest pattern that survives the constraints.

item.title: What Is Spec-Driven Development? The Spec as Source of Truth
item.description: For most of software history the spec was a temporary planning artifact and the code was ground truth. Spec-driven development inverts that: the versioned specification becomes the primary artifact, and code is generated or verified against it. The idea is old — formal methods, design-by-contract, BDD all contain versions. What’s new is the motive: AI agents need explicit, durable intent because prompts evaporate and sessions reset.

item.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns: Six Topologies and How Each Breaks
item.description: Single-agent systems peaked with bounded tasks and one prompt. Production moved on: organizations now run double-digit agent counts, and a large share of multi-agent pilots die within months of deployment. The killer isn’t the idea — it’s picking the wrong coordination topology, or the right one without knowing its failure modes.

item.title: Open WebUI: Self-Hosted ChatGPT Alternative for Local LLMs
item.description: Open WebUI brings the ChatGPT experience onto your own infrastructure: Ollama plus any OpenAI-compatible backend behind a modern chat UI with RAG document chat, multi-user auth, voice, prompt tooling, and model management. Privacy-first, offline-capable, and scalable from laptop Docker runs to Kubernetes fleets.

item.title: Ollama to vLLM: When Your Local Server Needs to Grow Up
item.description: Ollama is the easiest way to run a local model, until the experiment becomes a shared service. Requests queue, latency wobbles, prefixes recompute, and one GPU stops being enough. vLLM answers exactly those problems — but migration is a trade, not an upgrade: simplicity for scheduling, memory control, parallelism, and production operations.

item.title: Superpowers vs Agent Skills vs Pocock: Three Philosophies, One Measured Bake-Off
item.description: Three skill frameworks promise to make coding agents write better code: an autonomous pipeline, a full-lifecycle system with adversarial guards, and a requirements-first toolkit. Their repos differ in philosophy — and a measured same-feature bake-off puts numbers on the tradeoffs: 78 minutes and $34 against 148 minutes and $92.

item.title: The SDD Workflow: Five Phases from Requirements to Verified Code
item.description: Spec-driven development works when the specification is a workflow, not a document filed away after kickoff. The point is a sequence of reviewable artifacts — requirements, design, tasks, implementation, validation — each reducing ambiguity before anyone, human or agent, changes production code.

item.title: Pi Coding Agent Review: A Minimal Harness You Finish Yourself
item.description: Most coding agents keep getting bigger: planning modes, subagents, permission layers, IDE integrations, background workers. Pi walks the other way. Four default tools — read, write, edit, bash — with everything interesting left to extensions, skills, packages, and your own workflow. It is less a finished product than an editable harness, and that is exactly the point.

item.title: Claude Code with Local Backends: Install, Config, Ollama, and llama.cpp
item.description: Claude Code isn’t autocomplete with better marketing — it’s a terminal-native junior engineer that needs review. This guide covers install, settings layering, self-hosted Ollama and llama.cpp backends, pricing rails, and troubleshooting.

item.title: A2A and MCP Agent Security: Identity, Delegation, and Audit Trails
item.description: Prompt injection gets the attention, but it stops being the whole problem once agents call tools and delegate work. Identity, authorization, delegation limits, and audit trails become first-class architecture — not optional hardening.

item.title: Keeping Specs, Tests, and Code in Sync When Agents Write Fast
item.description: A spec nobody re-checks against the running system is worse than no spec: reviewers trust the document instead of the diff while the agent follows whatever the code actually does. Agents regenerate code fast, and each regeneration is a fresh chance for spec and implementation to diverge. The fix is a small enforceable link between requirement, design decision, tests, and the commits that changed them.

item.title: Decision Records: The Missing Memory Layer for AI Coding Agents
item.description: AI-generated code is cheap; judgment is scarce. When models write the code, nobody remembers why PostgreSQL beat DynamoDB, why AI emails must stay drafts, or why suggestions live in a side panel. Decision records — short, version-controlled documents capturing what was decided, why, and what was rejected — turn that judgment into durable project memory both humans and agents can read.

item.title: Spec Kit vs Kiro vs Claude Code: Picking an SDD Setup by Tradeoff, Not Hype
item.description: Developers comparing spec-driven setups in 2026 usually aren’t asking which model is smartest. They’re asking which workflow keeps an AI agent aligned without burying them in ceremony. Spec Kit, Kiro, and Claude Code custom workflows all implement specify-plan-tasks-implement-validate — but they bet differently on portability versus integration depth.

item.title: SDD vs Vibe Coding: Waterfall with Markdown or Controlled Iteration?
item.description: Spec-driven development entered 2026 as the serious developer’s answer to vibe coding drift: implement against a reviewed specification, not an ad-hoc prompt. Hacker News called it “Waterfall Strikes Back.” Both sides have a point — and the practical question was never which side wins, but how much spec a specific task needs.

item.title: Superpowers: Enforced Spec-Driven Skills for Coding Agents
item.description: Most spec-driven setups fail the same way: a solid plan-implement skill gets used diligently for a week, then quietly abandoned the first time a deadline gets close. Nothing in a hand-rolled skill stops that drift. Superpowers answers the discipline problem directly — a skills package that makes brainstorming, planning, subagent review, and strict TDD mandatory steps the agent checks before every task.

item.title: OpenCode CLI in Practice: Scriptable Agent Workflows That Hold Up
item.description: OpenCode’s command-line interface turns the coding agent into a scriptable tool: the same agent environment runs in the interactive TUI and non-interactively from shell scripts, CI jobs, and Makefiles. Small tasks work within minutes, but serious use depends on repository instructions, permission boundaries, context discipline, and model selection.

item.title: Agent Skills vs MCP Servers: Where Should the Responsibility Live?
item.description: Agent skills and MCP servers are often presented as competing ways to extend an AI agent. That framing is wrong: a skill teaches the agent how to work, while an MCP server gives it governed access to live capabilities. The useful question is not which standard wins, but where each responsibility should live.

item.title: Hugo llms.txt and Plain-Text Output for AI Agents on GitHub Pages
item.description: HTML is fine for humans in a browser. For AI agents it is often a pile of navigation, scripts, sidebars, and chrome wrapped around the few paragraphs that actually matter. If you run a technical Hugo site, you can serve a clean text sibling of every post plus a site-wide llms.txt index so agents skip the HTML tax.

item.title: AI for DevOps
item.description: AI is transforming DevOps practices through agentic AI systems that go beyond simple chatbots. These coding agents combine large language models with tools, memory, and planning capabilities to autonomously handle complex Platform Engineering and SRE tasks. By integrating with MCPs (Model Context Protocol), skills, and spec-driven development workflows, agents can create observability systems, build infrastructure APIs, and manage systems with minimal human intervention.

item.title: Future of DevOps in the AI World
item.description: If you have been doing DevOps long enough, you remember the shift from artisanal deploys to pipeline-as-code. The next shift will feel familiar in shape even if the ingredients look alien: we are still wiring stages, gates, and blast radius—but some stages will call models and tools, not only make and kubectl.

item.title: OpenSpec: The Spec-Driven Development Revolution
item.description: In the age of AI-assisted coding, one problem keeps surfacing: AI doesn’t follow instructions. OpenSpec changes that by introducing spec-driven development—a disciplined workflow where specifications are written before code is generated.

item.title: AI IDE Fundamentals: Agents, Commands, Skills, Rules, Context, and Workflows Explained
item.description: Modern AI-powered IDEs like Kilo Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot have introduced a new vocabulary: agents, skills, rules, contexts, and workflows. But what do these terms actually mean, and how do you use them effectively?

item.description: One of the most powerful features of Kilo Code is its ability to understand your entire codebase semantically—not just through keyword matching, but by grasping the actual meaning and relationships in your code.

item.description: In our first post, we introduced the core concepts of Kilo Code and why it’s a game-changer for agentic software development. Now, it’s time to get your hands dirty.

item.title: Kilo Code: The Future of Agentic Software Development
item.description: The world of AI coding is moving fast. We’ve seen the rise of simple autocomplete, then the transition to chat-based assistants, and now we are entering the era of Agentic AI.

item.title: VSCode AI Coding Plugins Compared: GitHub Copilot vs Continue.dev vs Kilo Code
item.description: AI-powered coding assistants have become essential tools for modern developers. In this post, I’ll compare three popular VSCode extensions: GitHub Copilot, Continue.dev, and Kilo Code (kilo.io), helping you choose the right one for your workflow.

item.title: AI IDE Core Concepts: Agents, Commands, Skills, Rules, Context, and Workflows
item.description: Modern AI-powered IDEs have evolved far beyond simple code completion. Today’s tools like Kilo Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity introduce new paradigms: autonomous agents, reusable skills, markdown rules, semantic context, and structured workflows.

item.title: AI Software Development: Spec-Driven vs. Vibe Coding
item.description: The early days of AI coding were characterized by “vibe coding”—a process where developers would prompt an LLM, hope for a working snippet, and manually fix the hallucinations. While fast for simple tasks, this approach often falls apart in complex, multi-file projects where “context rot” and technical debt accumulate rapidly.

item.title: AI IDE Configuration Standards: From .vscode to AGENTS.md
item.description: As AI tools become more integrated into our development workflows, the way we configure our projects is changing. We’ve moved beyond simple .gitignore and .env files into a world where we need to provide specific “instructions” and “context” to our AI assistants.

item.title: The Best AI Coding IDEs in 2026: VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, and More
item.description: The landscape of software development has shifted from “writing code with AI assistance” to “developing in AI-native environments.” While VS Code with GitHub Copilot remains the industry standard, a new breed of IDEs is challenging its dominance by integrating LLMs and autonomous agents into the very core of the editor.

item.title: The Best AI Coding CLIs in 2026: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and Qwen Code CLI
item.description: While AI-native IDEs like Cursor and Windsurf have taken the developer world by storm, a parallel revolution has been happening in the terminal. AI Coding CLIs (Command Line Interfaces) offer a different paradigm: they are lightweight, terminal-native, and often more “agentic” than their GUI counterparts.
